title: Redpine x Redwood — Security + Performance Review (data handling + benchmark methodology)
topics: How Redwood builds representative workload shapes without storing customer prompts
Telemetry/logging defaults and opt-outs (TTFT/TPOT, token counts, traces)
Benchmark suite methodology and reproducibility (artifact versioning, variance budgets)
Dedicated vs Private/VPC deployment options for regulated workloads
Security controls: encryption, KMS/HSM, audit logs, retention, access controls
summary: Redpine asked specifically how Redwood constructs the Q1'26 representative workload suite (prompt length distributions, cache hit scenarios, concurrency ramps) without ingesting or retaining sensitive customer prompts. Redwood clarified that the workload suite is based on aggregated, non-content metadata (token-length histograms, concurrency distributions, streaming vs non-streaming ratios) and synthetic/sanitized prompt sets; raw prompt text is not required. For any customer-specific validation, Redwood can run a benchmark harness in Redpine-controlled environments (Private/VPC) or accept customer-provided prompts only under explicit agreement and with tight retention/handling. Redwood also walked through telemetry: TTFT/TPOT and token counters can be collected without payload logging; content logging is disabled by default, and retention/fields are configurable by tier/deployment. Next steps include sending the security pack + DPA language, a one-pager on workload-shape capture, and scheduling a technical benchmark planning session.
questions: Do you ever store full prompts/responses for benchmarking or to build your workload taxonomy?
What exactly is collected for TTFT/TPOT and how do you prevent prompt text from showing up in traces/logs?
Can we run your benchmark harness inside our VPC / without internet egress?
How do you avoid re-identification when you say you use 'aggregated production signals'?
What retention periods apply to request metadata and performance metrics?
If we provide our prompts for a POC, what is the deletion process and who can access them?
next_steps: Redwood to send: security/compliance pack (SOC 2 report under NDA), data retention matrix, and logging/telemetry field list (owner: Henry Cho).

Redwood to send: one-pager describing 'representative traffic shapes' inputs (token-length histograms, concurrency, streaming ratio) and explicit statement that raw prompts are not required (owner: Noah Patel).
Set up a 45-min follow-up: benchmark planning session mapping Redpine traffic to suite shapes + identifying any customer-specific 'Shape R' to add (owner: Henry Cho).
Redpine to confirm preferred deployment for POC benchmarking (Hosted Dedicated vs Private/VPC) and any data residency constraints (owner: Maya R.).
If Redpine wants customer-prompt validation, Redwood to propose an in-VPC run approach with Redpine-provided prompt files that never leave their boundary (owner: Logan Wright).

Fireflies.ai Transcript

Meeting title: Redpine x Redwood — Security + Performance Review (data handling + benchmark methodology)
Date/time: 2026-03-04 2:00 PM PT
Duration: 63 minutes

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Henry Cho, Noah Patel, Logan Wright, Paula Mendes, Allison Grant
Redpine Fintech: Maya R. (Security Eng), Jordan K. (Platform), Elena V. (ML Eng), Sam P. (Vendor Risk)

---

[00:00] Henry Cho: Cool, thanks everyone for making time. The goal today is kind of combined security and performance review, and specifically the question you all sent over about, um, workload capture and whether any sensitive prompt data is stored.

[00:14] Maya R.: Yep. We’re okay sharing distributions, but we can’t have raw customer prompts leaving our boundary. Even “sampling” is a problem for us.

[00:23] Henry Cho: Totally understood. Maybe we start by separating two things: (1) what we collect in production telemetry for normal operations, and (2) what we use to build the representative workload suite and the Q1 baselines.

[00:35] Jordan K.: And (3) what happens in a POC if we want to validate your p99 claims with our exact workload.

[00:41] Henry Cho: Yep, exactly.

[00:44] Noah Patel: I can take the performance side. The baselines we’re publishing internally, and selectively externally, are not derived from customer prompt text. The “representative shapes” are basically: prompt token length distribution, output token distribution, streaming yes/no, concurrency regime (steady vs bursty), cache hit scenarios, and some multi-tenant mixing.

[01:04] Elena V.: When you say “derived from production signals,” that’s the part we’re nervous about.

[01:09] Noah Patel: Right. When we say production signals, we mean aggregated metrics like histograms of input token counts and output token counts, not payload. Like “p50 prompt length is 220 tokens, p95 is 1,800” type of thing. We don’t need the literal text to build the scheduling and kernel baselines.

[01:26] Logan Wright: And just to be explicit: our telemetry pipeline can operate with payload logging off. By default, for the hosted API, we record request metadata needed for billing and reliability, like token counts, model ID, region, timestamps, status codes. We do not need to store prompt content.

[01:43] Maya R.: Do you store it anyway? Like for debugging? Some vendors say “not by default” but it’s in some trace sample.

[01:50] Logan Wright: Good question. Content logging is disabled by default. There are two ways content can show up: (a) if a customer explicitly enables debug logging and sends it to their own sink, or (b) if the customer includes content in some header/metadata they pass, which we recommend against. Our standard tracing fields do not include prompt text.

[02:10] Allison Grant: And on the observability side, our guidance is “no high-cardinality or sensitive dimensions.” The dashboards are model/region/hardware/traffic shape, and the trace sampling is focused on timings and counters.

[02:23] Sam P.: I need a crisp statement for vendor risk: “Redwood does not store prompts and responses.” Is that accurate?

[02:32] Paula Mendes: The accurate statement is: Redwood does not require storing prompts/responses to provide the service and to produce the baseline suite; and content logging is off by default. For certain enterprise support scenarios, we can agree on a process if you choose to provide content for debugging, but it’s opt-in and governed by retention and access controls in the MSA/DPA.

[02:55] Sam P.: Okay, so default is no. Opt-in is possible under contract. Got it.

[03:02] Maya R.: For our policy, we’d want “cannot access content” not “doesn’t by default.” Can you do a VPC deployment where you literally can’t see it?

[03:11] Henry Cho: Yes, that’s Redwood Private in a customer VPC. There’s also Dedicated with stronger isolation, but Private is the “your network, your controls” model.

[03:20] Jordan K.: In Private, can we run the control plane ourselves? Or is it still calling home?

[03:27] Henry Cho: Private has a private control plane with customer-managed networking. There are options for limited egress, and we can walk through that with your network team.

[03:38] Noah Patel: And for benchmarking specifically, we can run the benchmark harness against a Private endpoint so your prompts never leave. The harness can run on your side or in the VPC.

[03:48] Elena V.: So the representative workload suite you’re building — it includes prompts though, right? Like you need actual strings to generate tokens.

[03:56] Noah Patel: Yes, you need strings, but they can be synthetic. We have synthetic prompt templates (documentation style, chatty style, code-ish style) and we calibrate lengths by tokenizing with the model tokenizer. The key part is the length distribution and turn structure, not the semantics.

[04:14] Elena V.: But semantics can affect caching and maybe attention patterns.

[04:18] Noah Patel: For kernel-level performance, semantics generally don’t matter; tensor shapes do. For caching, it’s more about prefix reuse patterns and cache hit rates. We simulate cache hit regimes by repeating prefixes, not by using real customer strings.

[04:32] Jordan K.: When you say “cache hit rate,” how do you measure that without storing the prompts?

[04:38] Logan Wright: You don’t need the prompt. You can measure cache hits via runtime counters and annotations per request: like whether a request had a prefix cache hit, partial hit, or miss; KV cache reuse ratio. It’s all internal state, not the payload.

[04:55] Maya R.: Are those annotations stored? Like per request log line.

[04:59] Logan Wright: They can be emitted as metrics aggregates (counters/histograms). In dedicated/private, you can control whether per-request logs are kept and for how long. In hosted, we keep operational logs with retention limits, but again it’s not prompt text.

[05:14] Sam P.: Can you list exactly what is retained and for how long? We’ll need that.

[05:18] Henry Cho: Yes. We have a retention matrix by product tier. We’ll send it.

[05:23] Noah Patel: If it helps, the baseline project we’re doing this quarter is trying to make this very explicit: what we measure (TTFT, TPOT, end-to-end), what’s variance vs regression, and what metadata is needed.

[05:36] Elena V.: Let’s talk TTFT. We saw some discrepancy with another vendor where TTFT looked great server-side but client experience was worse.

[05:44] Logan Wright: Yeah. We’ve been validating that. For streaming, TTFT can be tricky because “first token” vs “first chunk” vs client receiving bytes. We record server-side timestamps (request received, first token produced, first chunk flushed), and you can also instrument client-side. We’ve been building a validation harness that compares them.

[06:04] Maya R.: Does any of that include the content? Like the first chunk itself?

[06:08] Logan Wright: No, it’s timestamps and sizes, not the text.

[06:12] Jordan K.: Can you share those definitions? Like what is your TTFT exactly.

[06:16] Noah Patel: Yes. We have a methodology doc. In the baseline suite, TTFT is “request received by runtime to first token made available to stream,” plus we include “first byte to client” when possible in the harness. We can share the formal definition we’re using.

[06:34] [crosstalk]

[06:35] Henry Cho: Sorry, go ahead Maya.

[06:37] Maya R.: On the re-identification thing. You said histograms. But if you have a unique prompt length and model and time window, could that be re-identified?

[06:49] Allison Grant: That’s why we don’t put those into high-cardinality dimensions. Internally we aggregate across windows and enforce minimum bucket counts. Also, for anything we describe as “representative shapes,” it’s not a report of a specific customer; it’s a blended taxonomy across many workloads.

[07:06] Noah Patel: Also, the shapes are intentionally coarse. Like “short chat,” “mixed prompts,” “long context streaming,” “bursty concurrency.” They’re not per-customer fingerprints.

[07:16] Elena V.: But you do have a “long context streaming” shape because customers do that.

[07:20] Noah Patel: Yes, lots of folks do it. But the definition is like: prompts 8k-32k, output 200-800, streaming on, concurrency ramp 5 to 50, cache warm/cold phases. Not “Redpine’s prompt.”

[07:37] Sam P.: Okay. For compliance, you mentioned SOC 2. Do you have it?

[07:41] Henry Cho: Yes, we can share under NDA. We’ll send the package.

[07:47] Maya R.: How about encryption and key management? For hosted and for dedicated.

[07:52] Paula Mendes: Hosted: encryption in transit and at rest. Dedicated and Private: we have KMS integrations; for Private you can use your own KMS/HSM depending on cloud. Audit logs are available for admin actions.

[08:08] Jordan K.: Is there an option for “no logs leave the VPC” for Private?

[08:12] Henry Cho: Yes, the private deployment can be configured so logs go to your sink only. There is still operational telemetry that helps health, but we can constrain it. We’d want to get your exact requirement documented.

[08:26] Maya R.: We’d want “no payload, no prompts, no responses, no embeddings” leaving. Metrics are okay.

[08:31] Logan Wright: Embeddings are payload too, yeah. In Private, we can design it so payload stays in your network. Metrics can be aggregates only.

[08:41] Elena V.: Back to benchmarking: you said you can run harness in our VPC. How does that work? Is it like a container?

[08:49] Noah Patel: It’s basically a runner CLI that takes a workload config: shapes, seeds, model, region, concurrency. It generates synthetic prompts or uses provided prompt files. It measures TTFT/TPOT/throughput and writes artifacts. We can provide it as a container image or you can build from source.

[09:08] Jordan K.: If we provide prompt files, do you ever upload them to your systems?

[09:12] Noah Patel: If you run it inside your environment, no. If you ask us to run it in ours, then that’s a separate process and we would need written approval, strict retention, and access controls. But the preferred model for you is: it runs in your VPC.

[09:30] Maya R.: That’s what we want. We want to validate your latency on our prompts without you seeing our prompts.

[09:36] Henry Cho: That lines up. We can propose a Private POC, or a Dedicated endpoint inside a private network path depending on what you prefer.

[09:46] Sam P.: Wait, Dedicated is still hosted by you though, right?

[09:49] Henry Cho: Dedicated is Redwood-managed but isolated capacity. Private is the one where you have customer-managed networking and tighter control. For the strictest boundary, Private.

[10:03] Elena V.: We also care about p99 under bursts. We’ve had issues where decode stalls when concurrency spikes.

[10:10] Noah Patel: That’s one of the shapes in the suite: bursty concurrency with mixed prompt lengths. It tends to expose scheduler fairness issues and backpressure.

[10:20] Jordan K.: Do you have metrics we can monitor that explain p99? Like queue depth, batch size, stuff like that.

[10:26] Allison Grant: Yes. We’re standardizing scheduler metrics: queue wait time histograms, batch composition, prefill vs decode utilization, backpressure counters. Those are used to interpret tail latency.

[10:40] Maya R.: Are those exposed to customers or internal only?

[10:43] Henry Cho: In Dedicated/Private, we can expose more. Hosted, we expose a subset via Console, and some deeper metrics are available with enterprise observability options. We can align on what you need.

[10:58] Elena V.: Sorry, I’m going to ask directly: do you train on customer data.

[11:02] Henry Cho: No. Redwood is an inference platform. We do not use customer prompts/responses to train models.

[11:09] Maya R.: Okay.

[11:10] Sam P.: And you said you don’t store prompts by default, but do you have an incident process if something leaks into logs.

[11:18] Logan Wright: Yes. We have detection for unexpected payload-like strings in logs, plus access controls, and an incident response process. But the design intent is that payload never enters logs. We also advise customers not to put payload in headers or request IDs.

[11:37] Jordan K.: On request IDs—some systems accidentally include user identifiers there.

[11:41] Allison Grant: Exactly. We recommend opaque UUIDs. For enterprise setups, we can help with that integration.

[11:49] Henry Cho: Maybe we shift to “what would you need to be comfortable” for the POC.

[11:55] Maya R.: For me: DPA language that says no prompt/response storage, retention period for metadata, access control, and ability to run the benchmark inside our VPC.

[12:06] Sam P.: And SOC 2 report, plus subprocessor list.

[12:10] Henry Cho: Yep.

[12:12] Elena V.: And a clear mapping of our workload to your suite shapes. We want to know you’re not cherry-picking.

[12:20] Noah Patel: Totally. We actually do that in the suite: we publish the full workload config and seeds and the environment pinning (driver/CUDA/runtime build). That’s how we avoid “it ran on a magic GPU.”

[12:35] Jordan K.: That’s great, but also scary because it means you have a bunch of configs. Where are those stored?

[12:41] Noah Patel: In a versioned repo with tags. And the artifacts include the metadata, like commit SHA and driver versions. Again, nothing sensitive in there.

[12:52] Maya R.: So you don’t store prompts, but you store configs. Fine.

[12:55] Logan Wright: Right. The configs are “shape definitions,” not payload.

[13:02] Sam P.: For privacy, do you do any k-anonymity or differential privacy or something.

[13:08] Logan Wright: For the aggregated signals that inform general shapes, we enforce minimum aggregation thresholds and coarse bucketization. We’re not applying formal DP today for that taxonomy, but the data used is not content and is not per-customer visible.

[13:23] Maya R.: I’d like that in writing: “not formal DP, but aggregated and bucketed.”

[13:27] Henry Cho: We can write it up clearly.

[13:31] Elena V.: Another concern: if you’re doing tokenization to get lengths, tokenization depends on text. If we run in our VPC, you’ll have our text in memory.

[13:41] Noah Patel: Yes, but in your environment. The process will obviously have the text in memory to send it to the model, but it won’t be persisted. And the harness can be configured to not write the prompts to disk.

[13:55] Jordan K.: Do you have a way to prove it’s not writing to disk.

[13:58] Noah Patel: We can provide the source and container manifest. And if you run it, you can restrict filesystem permissions and egress.

[14:08] Maya R.: Okay.

[14:09] Henry Cho: Let me check if there are any other open questions before we go deeper on performance numbers.

[14:15] Sam P.: One more: data residency. Can we keep everything in us-east only.

[14:20] Henry Cho: Yes, we can pin region. Private obviously is in your chosen region.

[14:26] Noah Patel: Performance baselines are also region-specific because fleet variance is real, so we report by region and hardware.

[14:34] Elena V.: Hardware: what GPUs are you using for the baseline suite.

[14:38] Noah Patel: Depends on the model, but for the top-served set we include H100 class and some A100 class where relevant. We lock driver/CUDA versions per run.

[14:50] Jordan K.: If our POC is on different hardware, the baseline might not match.

[14:54] Noah Patel: Right, that’s why we do normalization and we keep baselines per hardware SKU. For your p99 requirement, we’d recommend testing on the target SKU.

[15:06] Maya R.: How do you handle multi-tenant noise in Dedicated.

[15:10] Henry Cho: Dedicated is isolated capacity—single tenant. The multi-tenant shapes in the suite are for hosted, where you see mixed workloads. For your case, likely dedicated/private shapes are more relevant.

[15:23] Elena V.: Can I ask about “streaming TTFT”? Like if the server sends an empty chunk first.

[15:28] Logan Wright: Yeah, that was a bug we fixed recently in our instrumentation. We now record first token and first non-empty chunk separately. The harness can validate it.

[15:40] Jordan K.: Great. Because we’ve had vendors game that.

[15:43] Henry Cho: Understood.

[15:45] (brief pause)

[15:46] Henry Cho: Noah, do you want to walk them through what a benchmark run would look like for Redpine.

[15:52] Noah Patel: Sure. We’d start by mapping your traffic into, say, two or three shapes. Example: “streaming chat short,” “streaming chat long context,” “bursty concurrency mixed lengths.” Then we pick model candidates, quantization profile if any, and set acceptance: p95, p99 TTFT and TPOT, plus throughput under concurrency.

[16:14] Elena V.: We also have a reranker, but that’s less strict.

[16:17] Noah Patel: Okay, we can include it but keep the main focus on chat.

[16:21] Jordan K.: What do you need from us to define the shape.

[16:25] Noah Patel: You can provide distributions without content: histogram of prompt tokens, output tokens, percent streaming, concurrency over time. Even just “typical,” “busy hour,” “peak burst.”

[16:39] Maya R.: That data itself can be sensitive but less so.

[16:43] Noah Patel: Right. And you can generalize it further.

[16:46] Logan Wright: Also, for token counts, you can compute them on your side using the model tokenizer if you want. You don’t have to send us raw text.

[16:57] Elena V.: That’s a good idea.

[17:00] Sam P.: If we share distributions, do you store them.

[17:04] Henry Cho: If you email a spreadsheet, it exists in email, yes. But we can also do it verbally and put only generalized numbers in notes. Or we can store it in your doc system. We can align with your preference.

[17:19] Maya R.: Let’s do it in our doc system.

[17:21] Henry Cho: Works for us.

[17:24] (crosstalk)

[17:25] Jordan K.: One last question on the representative suite. You said it’s synthetic prompts. Do you ever use “sanitized prompts” from customers.

[17:33] Noah Patel: Not as a default input. The phrase “sanitized” for us means: sometimes we take public domain text or Redwood-authored prompts and remove anything that looks like secrets, PII, customer identifiers. We’re not taking customer prompts and trying to sanitize them. For any customer-specific prompt set, we’d keep it customer-controlled.

[17:53] Maya R.: That’s the key. We don’t want you sanitizing our stuff, we want you not having it.

[17:58] Noah Patel: Exactly.

[18:00] Henry Cho: Okay. I think we hit the main concern. Paula, can you cover contract language options.

[18:06] Paula Mendes: Sure. We can include data handling commitments in the DPA: no training, no prompt/response retention, limited metadata retention, access controls, and deletion SLAs. For Private deployments, we can specify that payload does not leave customer network, and logs are customer-managed.

[18:28] Sam P.: Deletion SLA meaning “if we terminate, you delete within X days.”

[18:32] Paula Mendes: Yes, plus backups. We can share the standard terms.

[18:38] Maya R.: Great.

[18:40] Henry Cho: We’re at about 20 minutes. Let’s do a quick recap of what we’re sending and set the next meeting.

[18:46] Henry Cho: Items on our side: security pack + SOC2 under NDA, retention matrix, list of telemetry fields, and a one-pager on workload-shape capture emphasizing no raw prompts needed.

[18:58] Maya R.: And the benchmark harness can be run in our VPC.

[19:01] Noah Patel: Yes.

[19:02] Jordan K.: Can we schedule the benchmark planning session next week.

[19:06] Henry Cho: Yes, I’ll send options.

[19:09] (Transcript continues with deeper Q&A on retention, access controls, and benchmarking logistics; minor transcription gaps)

[19:18] Elena V.: On access control, who at Redwood can access logs.

[19:22] Logan Wright: Least privilege. On hosted, SRE/oncall has access to operational logs with audited access. For enterprise, we can restrict further and provide audit logs. For Private, it’s your log sink.

[19:38] Maya R.: Do you support SSO and RBAC in the console.

[19:42] Henry Cho: Yes. SAML/SSO and RBAC.

[19:46] Sam P.: Subprocessors, please.

[19:48] Henry Cho: Yep.

[19:51] Jordan K.: If we do Private, do you still have remote access for support.

[19:56] Henry Cho: It’s configurable. Some customers allow break-glass with approval. Others do fully customer-operated. We can discuss your requirements.

[20:10] Maya R.: We’re closer to “no remote access.”

[20:12] Henry Cho: Understood.

[20:15] Noah Patel: For performance troubleshooting in that mode, we rely on metrics and artifacts you can export (without payload). Like profiles, kernel timings, scheduler metrics.

[20:28] Elena V.: And those artifacts don’t contain prompts.

[20:31] Noah Patel: Correct. Profilers show kernel timelines and shapes, not text.

[20:38] Jordan K.: Okay.

[20:40] Henry Cho: I think we’re good. Anything else before we wrap.

[20:44] Sam P.: No, just send the docs.

[20:46] Maya R.: And please put the “no prompt storage” language in a clean statement.

[20:51] Henry Cho: Will do.
